title: Bhai Taru Singh, 1745
hookLine: a young farmer who fed travelers refuses to cut his hair even under torture

lines: A KNOCK AT THE DOOR, LATE.
cards: A knock at the door, late at night. On the step, two strangers, thin, dusty, clearly on the run. Everyone in the village knows feeding people like this is dangerous.
Somebody might be watching. Somebody might talk. You could say you have nothing and close the door, and nobody would ever blame you.
In a small village near Lahore in the 1740s, a young farmer heard knocks like that again and again. He never closed the door. Today: Bhai Taru Singh.

teach.h: A FARMER WHO FED THE HUNTED.
teach.b: Taru Singh was a young farmer who lived with his mother and sister in Poohla, a village not far from Lahore. These were the years of the price on Sikh heads. The Khalsa bands hid in the jungles, and they needed food.
Taru Singh grew grain and shared it. Travelers, hunted Sikhs, anyone hungry at the door: tradition says his household fed them all, from the little they had. Someone informed on him.
In 1745 he was arrested and brought before the governor in Lahore, charged with feeding the rebels.

He was offered his life if he gave up his faith and cut his hair. He said his kesh, his uncut hair, was part of his faith, and he would keep it along with his life's breath. The governor's men removed his scalp.
Tradition says he bore it with his lips moving in prayer, and died soon after.
Sikhs remember him in Ardas among those who were scalped rather than give up their kesh. You'll remember kesh from the five Ks: hair kept as it was given. For Taru Singh it wasn't a rule.
It was himself. Now, the week. The battle inside: the real battle.
Banda Singh Bahadur: called to serve. Sirhind: land to the tillers. Banda's end: true to the end.
The years in the forests: they survived. Bhai Mani Singh: the scribe stood firm.
And Bhai Taru Singh, the farmer who kept feeding strangers, and kept his kesh.

how: Sikhs remember Bhai Taru Singh in Ardas among those who gave their scalps rather than their kesh; a gurdwara, Shaheed Ganj Bhai Taru Singh, marks the place in Lahore, and his story is often told to children to explain why Sikhs keep their hair.

games.q: the 1740s. there's a price on Sikh heads. two hungry strangers on the run knock at your door at night. what do you do?
o: say you have nothing, and close the door.
feed them, from the little you have.
games.why: tradition says Taru Singh's household fed everyone who came. it's what he was arrested for.

practice: Think of someone who could use a meal right now: a friend with a new baby, a coworker on a long shift, a neighbor living alone, someone passing through a hard stretch.
Picture them at your door, and what you'd set in front of them, a meal, a snack, a coffee, a place at your table. Stay with that open door for a few quiet breaths.

wordCard.voice: Kesh. Uncut hair, part of the faith of Bhai Taru Singh, the young farmer who fed hunted Sikhs and travelers, and in 1745 refused to cut it to save his life.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kesh (kes), uncut hair, one of the five Ks.

carryVoice: Your line: he kept his kesh. And he never closed the door. That's the week, and day two hundred eighty-seven.
